title: A mean-and-variance homogenised DOISST v2.1 makes the 2023/24 SST record jump 0.20-0.22 C (not 0.25 C) and 1.3-3 times less rare, and lowers 1982-2025 heatwave-day trends by 19-22% (60S-60N)
abstract: Question: NOAA Daily OISST v2.1 (DOISST) has steps in its mean (1985, 2005, an undocumented step on 2020-07-07, and a fixed ship adjustment) and in its day-to-day variance at satellite-input changes. Which published marine climate results survive when both artifacts are removed? Approach: we fitted regional step models of DOISST minus three references of different types (ESA CCI v3.0.1 at the same 29,129 one-degree cells and days, ERSSTv5, HadSST4.2), applied them with a variance homogenisation (spectral matching below about 32 days), and recomputed the record-jump statistics of Terhaar et al. (2025), Hobday heatwave and cold-spell statistics and the 2023 records. We tested the corrections by cross-validation, at 128 moored buoys not used in the fits, and with placebo dates. Results: raw DOISST reproduces the published 2023/24 60S-60N jump (0.249 C), end trend (0.269 C per decade) and return period (mean 501 against 512 years). The corrected records give a jump of 0.199-0.225 C, a trend of 0.214-0.219 C per decade and a mean return period of 167-400 years; the reference products give 0.196-0.217 C and 149-420 years. The 1982-2023 warming falls from 0.180 to 0.135-0.146 C per decade. The 1982-2025 heatwave-day trend falls from 21.2 to 16.5-17.2 days per year per decade (mean part), duration from 4.45 to 2.41-2.48 days per decade (variance part), the frequency trend does not change, peak intensity rises from 0.084 to 0.128-0.134 C per decade, and cold-spell lengthening disappears. 2023 stays the record heatwave year, with 16% fewer heatwave days. The 2020 step (+0.08 to +0.10 C) is large-scale and does not depend on in situ data density; its cause is unknown. Limitations: moorings confirm the step dates and signs, but at mooring sites the regional corrections remove about twice the observed trend excess; the references have their own errors.
